scenes.tts: How can one cell become two without leaving either new cell with half a chromosome set? Watch one blue chromosome through the whole answer. Its partners will stay visible, but blue is our guide.
scenes.visual: Hook before title. Fill the frame with one large schematic animal cell. COLOR MAP for both films: the guide chromosome BLUE and its partner LIGHT BLUE (one pair), the other pair ORANGE and LIGHT ORANGE, spindle fibers GREEN, nuclear envelopes YELLOW, cell boundary TEAL, phase labels TEXT. Show four simple chromosome rods; spotlight the BLUE rod. The cell begins stretching toward two faded daughter outlines while a large question mark opens between them. Keep all objects moving gently.
scenes.narration: How can one cell become two without leaving either new cell with half a chromosome set? Watch one blue chromosome through the whole answer. Its partners will stay visible, but blue is our guide.

scenes.visual: Brief title card after the hook: How One Set Becomes Two. Keep the blue guide chromosome beside the title, slowly rotating. No subtitle.

scenes.tts: A new cell enters G one, where it grows and does its everyday work. This busy stretch is interphase, not a rest. Next comes S phase, when the cell copies its D N A. G two prepares the cell to divide.
scenes.caption: A new cell enters G1, where it grows and does its everyday work. This busy stretch is interphase, not a rest. Next comes S phase, when the cell copies its DNA. G2 prepares the cell to divide.
scenes.visual: Return to the same schematic cell. Build one circular timeline around it, labelled G1, S, G2, M. Enlarge the cell during G1. Move a bright tracker through the three interphase arcs while the chromosomes remain loose inside a yellow nucleus. Place no numerical durations on the timeline.
scenes.narration: A new cell enters G1, where it grows and does its everyday work. This busy stretch is interphase, not a rest. Next comes S phase, when the cell copies its DNA. G2 prepares the cell to divide.

scenes.tts: During S phase, every chromosome is copied. The blue rod becomes two matching blue sister chromatids joined at one centromere. Its partners copy too. The D N A amount doubles, but each joined pair still counts as one copied chromosome.
scenes.caption: During S phase, every chromosome is copied. The blue rod becomes two matching blue sister chromatids joined at one centromere. Its partners copy too. The DNA amount doubles, but each joined pair still counts as one copied chromosome.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the yellow nucleus. Transform each loose chromosome rod into two identical joined rods. Make the blue guide copy first, then the other chromosome colors. Add one small centromere ring where each pair joins. Keep a visual counter: chromosome units unchanged; DNA copies doubled. Put the counters on screen without speaking their values.
scenes.narration: During S phase, every chromosome is copied. The blue rod becomes two matching blue sister chromatids joined at one centromere. Its partners copy too. The DNA amount doubles, but each joined pair still counts as one copied chromosome.

scenes.tts: Soon the copied chromosomes will line up across the cell's middle. Where must the two blue sister chromatids go so both new nuclei receive a complete set? Hold your answer.
scenes.visual: Move the copied chromosomes into one vertical row at the cell equator. Put a blue arrow stub on each sister chromatid, but leave both directions blank. Show the question at the top. Keep the chromosomes gently flexing while the question remains.
scenes.narration: Soon the copied chromosomes will line up across the cell's middle. Where must the two blue sister chromatids go so both new nuclei receive a complete set? Hold your answer.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the metaphase row, the two blank blue arrow stubs and the question visible. Pulse the two future poles softly; do not reveal directions.

scenes.tts: The blue copies must move to opposite poles. The same is true for every copied chromosome. Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one. That rule preserves the chromosome set through a typical mitotic division.
scenes.visual: Reveal opposite arrow directions on the blue sisters, then on every pair. Pull translucent matching chromosome-set outlines toward both poles, but do not move the chromosomes yet. Display the guiding rule once beside the cell, then shrink it into a small rule badge for the remaining scenes.
scenes.narration: The blue copies must move to opposite poles. The same is true for every copied chromosome. Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one. That rule preserves the chromosome set through a typical mitotic division.

scenes.tts: M phase begins with mitosis, division of the nucleus. In prophase, the copied chromosomes coil into thick visible shapes. Green spindle fibers form. Near the end, the yellow nuclear envelope breaks down, opening access to the chromosomes.
scenes.visual: Reset to early M phase in the same cell. Coil each joined pair into a compact X-like cartoon, clearly labelled schematic. Grow green spindle fibers from opposite poles. Break the yellow nuclear envelope into moving fragments near the end. Keep the blue guide pair prominent.
scenes.narration: M phase begins with mitosis, division of the nucleus. In prophase, the copied chromosomes coil into thick visible shapes. Green spindle fibers form. Near the end, the yellow nuclear envelope breaks down, opening access to the chromosomes.

scenes.tts: In metaphase, spindle fibers line the copied chromosomes across the middle. Each sister chromatid faces a different pole. The row is not the goal. It is the setup that lets matching copies move in opposite directions.
scenes.visual: Attach green spindle fibers to opposite sides of each joined pair and slide the pairs into one equatorial row. Use faint destination lanes, each in its chromosome's color, leading to opposite poles. Keep fiber tips moving as they settle; do not separate sisters yet.
scenes.narration: In metaphase, spindle fibers line the copied chromosomes across the middle. Each sister chromatid faces a different pole. The row is not the goal. It is the setup that lets matching copies move in opposite directions.

scenes.tts: In anaphase, the sister chromatids separate at their centromeres. Spindle fibers pull one copy of every chromosome toward each pole. Follow blue. One blue copy moves left, while its match moves right. Each separated chromatid now counts as a chromosome.
scenes.visual: Open every centromere ring. Pull matching chromatids along the green fibers toward opposite poles. Keep a blue trail behind the guide copies so their paths remain obvious. Change the on-screen label from sister chromatid to chromosome only after separation.
scenes.narration: In anaphase, the sister chromatids separate at their centromeres. Spindle fibers pull one copy of every chromosome toward each pole. Follow blue. One blue copy moves left, while its match moves right. Each separated chromatid now counts as a chromosome.

scenes.tts: In telophase, a complete set reaches each end. Yellow nuclear envelopes form, and the chromosomes loosen. Mitosis has made two nuclei. Cytokinesis often begins in late anaphase or telophase. It divides the cytoplasm. An animal cell pinches inward; a plant cell builds a plate outward into a new wall.
scenes.visual: Wrap each matching set in a new yellow envelope and loosen the chromosome shapes. Split the frame briefly: keep the carried animal cell pinching along a TEAL furrow; beside it, show a rectangular plant cell with a central TEAL plate growing outward. Label mitosis as nuclear division and cytokinesis as cytoplasmic division. End with matching chromosome sets glowing in both new nuclei.
scenes.narration: In telophase, a complete set reaches each end. Yellow nuclear envelopes form, and the chromosomes loosen. Mitosis has made two nuclei. Cytokinesis often begins in late anaphase or telophase. It divides the cytoplasm. An animal cell pinches inward; a plant cell builds a plate outward into a new wall.

scenes.tts: Notice what did not happen. The cell did not split its original chromosomes in half. It copied every chromosome before separation. That is why each finished nucleus can receive a complete set, not a random half.
scenes.visual: Place the starting cell above the two finished nuclei. Cross out a picture of original chromosomes cut into unmatched halves. Beside it, animate copied blue chromosomes separating into two matched sets. Let the two complete sets fill most of the frame, then fade everything for the end card.
scenes.narration: Notice what did not happen. The cell did not split its original chromosomes in half. It copied every chromosome before separation. That is why each finished nucleus can receive a complete set, not a random half.

scenes.visual: Clear the frame. Show one centered line only, with no title or smaller text: 'Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one.'
